newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch money market focused on year-end trade.
newsitem.headline: Dutch money market focused on year-end trade.

text.p: Monday's allocation under the new special advances pact, described as ample by dealers, pushed Dutch call money rates down a couple of basis points, with trades noted at 3.00 percent.

The Central Bank earlier allocated 7.74 billion guilders or 23.5 percent of the bank's individual applications under a one-day pact at 2.50 percent which replaced a six-day facility of 5.81 billion guilders.
Monday's pact was of a particularly short duration, as had been expected by some dealers before it was announced on Friday.
"Under such a short pact, the Central Bank can influence the call rate on an almost daily basis, thus avoiding too big a rise in overnight money," one dealer said.
One-week deposits were still very much in demand. They were bid between 3.25 and 3.30 percent and dealers said they changed hands at around the same price level.
Deposits running from December 31 to January 2 were also very active, trading at around five percent, up from 4.75 percent last Friday.
Other money market rates were broadly unchanged from Friday.
Unlike the bond and share markets, the Dutch money market will be open tomorrow, when the central bank will announce the allocation of its last special advances pact of 1996.
The terms of this new pact will be announced this afternoon, and the market is expecting it to be at an unchanged rate of 2.50 percent.
"Nothing has changed, there is no reason to hike the rate," said one trader.
Dealers expect the pact to be of a short duration again, but differ on its exact end date.

Some think it will last until the end of next week, while others expect it to run only until January 2, given the fact that starting next year, the Finance Ministry will join the central bank as an operator in the Dutch money market.
